comments.text: Public transportation looks cheap on paper but it only covers a small fraction of Mexico City. And the tourist friendly areas Roma Norte and La Condesa are very small. The Metro subway system is cheap, but, the LAST MILE TO or FROM your destination is unreliable and difficult to complete. It is one of the multiple reasons why punctuality in Mexico is an abstract concept. Public transportation is cheap, but unsafe, if you get your wallet, phone, or IDs due to lack of law enforcement presence IS NOT worth the risk. If your field of work allows you to work remotely and you can afford to mostly stay put with a few trips to the store every now and then it makes sense to move to Mexico City. But, if for any reason you have to commute you have to be aware that Mexico City is the most congested place in the world. The average driver commuting to work looses 152 hrs a year stuck in traffic according to the GPS Index. Not only that, gas in Mexico City is more expensive than the national average in the US. If you are using public transportation to get to work far away the time loss is far worse. There are people from neighboring states coming to work in Mexico City with 2 to 3 hrs spent on the road every day. Public protests and road blockages make “carmageddon” a frequent occurrence. Also the regular work week for the average Mexican looks like 48 hrs weekly, and, if you count the commuting time it looks more like 60 hrs. If you are a foreigner and you can arrange living close to work, traveling expectations at a reasonable level, or work from home in Mexico City it makes sense to move to here. If not, then your standard of living will be far worse than in an American city.

replies.author: @CarlosF-u3y
replies.text:
Mexican here, this is inaccurate. 

No housing is provided (homelessness is a major problem in our country). Pension isn't guaranteed and people don't even trust the system as the government has stolen pensions of thousands of retirees, leaving them without money. We do have a bonus (PTU) which is 10% of a company profits that is shared amongst workers, although this only applies to formal jobs (most people work in informal jobs). We technically do have universal health care but hospitals frequently run low on medications and caretakers, and it can take years just to get a surgery, so it's not unheard of people dying while waiting for a test or a procedure (and those who can go into the private sector and fall into medical debt). Education in public schools is indeed free or costs next to nothing in public university, and that's the only good thing we have.

replies.author: @CarlosF-u3y
replies.text:
Private healthcare is good, public healthcare is a coin flip. 

You can get a free doctor consultation but it's usually a whole day of waiting for urgent visits, and seeing a specialist can take months, so many people will opt for the private sector (that's why pharmacy clinics have been a life-saver for much of us, since a normal doctor easily runs for $50). However, if you've an emergency and you're unlucky, you can die while waiting to be seen by doctors in a public hospital, so people are willing to go into medical debt by going to a private hospital (I once spent over $1,500 just for an emergency stomachache, basically almost 3 months of my salary).
